title: Which data ingestion tool fits you?

questions.hint: Vendor-run tools charge by a meter. Open-source tools ask for your time.

options.label: A vendor runs it for me
options.why: you want the vendor to run it

options.label: My team runs it on our own servers
options.why: you are happy to run it yourself

options.label: A cloud service inside AWS
options.why: you want billing and access to stay inside AWS

questions.q: Where does your data come from?

options.label: Mostly SaaS apps
options.why: your sources are mostly SaaS apps

options.label: A mix of both
options.why: you have both apps and databases

questions.q: How fresh does the data need to be?
Where does the data need to land?

options.label: Apache Iceberg tables I control
options.why: you want Iceberg tables on your own storage

questions.q: What does your team know best?

options.label: Docker or Kubernetes
options.why: you can run Docker or Helm

fivetran.name: Fivetran
fivetran.summary: A vendor-run tool with 700+ connectors and a free plan.
fivetran.bestWhen: You want someone else to run the pipeline and can budget for the meter.
fivetran.watchOut: It bills by monthly active rows, deleted rows count, and self-hosting is limited (hybrid is listed under Enterprise).

hevo.name: Hevo
hevo.summary: No-code pipelines into a warehouse, with a free plan.
hevo.bestWhen: You are a small team that wants point-and-click setup.
hevo.watchOut: Every update is an event, and it publishes no self-hosted edition. Its Iceberg option is Early Access and Snowflake only.

airbyte.name: Airbyte
airbyte.summary: Over 600 connectors and a free self-hosted core that writes Iceberg to S3 and Google Cloud Storage.
airbyte.bestWhen: You want lots of connectors and can live with minutes to an hour of delay.
airbyte.watchOut: CDC runs on a schedule, and its Elastic License 2.0 is source-available, not strict open source.

dlt.name: dlt
dlt.summary: A Python library where ingestion pipelines live in your own repository.
dlt.bestWhen: Your team writes Python and wants full control.
dlt.watchOut: You write and maintain the code, and the paid dltHub plan is a flat monthly fee.

debezium.name: Debezium
debezium.summary: A free engine that reads database change logs and emits each change as an event.
debezium.bestWhen: Kafka is already in your stack and you want one stream for many readers.
debezium.watchOut: It is an engine you build a pipeline around, and somebody has to run it.

olake.name: OLake Go
olake.summary: It copies database changes into Apache Iceberg or Parquet on storage and a catalog you control.
olake.bestWhen: You run PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB or SQL Server and want Iceberg tables you control.
olake.watchOut: Scope: built for Iceberg and Parquet output, with change capture for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and SQL Server, run on your own infrastructure.

estuary.name: Estuary
estuary.summary: One vendor-run platform for streaming, change capture and batch.
estuary.bestWhen: You want streaming and batch from one vendor and can budget for instance fees.
estuary.watchOut: Each source and destination is a billed instance, and its Iceberg output needs Spark on AWS.

glue.name: AWS Glue
glue.summary: A serverless Spark service that can read and write Iceberg tables on S3.
glue.bestWhen: Your data and skills are already on AWS and you need transformation.
glue.watchOut: It needs Spark jobs, runs on AWS only, and we found no log-based CDC engine in its docs.
